goldens.comment: Unsafe raw List deserialization without type safety. Calling Optional.get() directly on the Optional returned by RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) without checking isPresent() can lead to a NoSuchElementException if the Optional is empty.

adjudication_records.issue_text: testsuite/.../federation/BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.java:339 — isValid() for RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE checks anyMatch against the full stored code list but never removes/marks the matched code as used, so a userStorage-backed recovery code is infinitely reusable (no single-use enforcement)

adjudication.rationale: In `BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid(...)`, the newly added `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE` branch deserializes the stored JSON list and returns `generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse()))` without updating the stored credential data to remove/mark the matched code as used. Nothing else in this diff shows any follow-up mutation of `myUser.recoveryCodes`, so a valid recovery code would remain valid indefinitely for this user-storage-backed implementation.

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/forms/login/freemarker/model/RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean.java:19 — credentialModelOpt.get()` is called without checking `isPresent()`, so if the user has no recovery-codes credential (e.g. race/inconsistent state) this throws `NoSuchElementException` instead of a handled error

adjudication.rationale: In `RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean`, the new code fetches `Optional<CredentialModel> credentialModelOpt = RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user);` and then immediately calls `credentialModelOpt.get()` without checking presence. Since `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential()` can return `Optional.empty()` when the user has no recovery-codes credential (it just searches federated then local streams), this can throw `NoSuchElementException` at runtime instead of being handled.

adjudication_records.issue_text: server-spi-private/src/main/java/org/keycloak/utils/CredentialHelper.java:127 — recoveryCodeCredentialProvider from session.getProvider(CredentialProvider.class, "keycloak-recovery-authn-codes") is used without a null check, so a missing provider registration causes an unhandled NullPointerException in the credential-creation path

adjudication.rationale: In `CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential(...)`, the code obtains `recoveryCodeCredentialProvider` via `session.getProvider(CredentialProvider.class, "keycloak-recovery-authn-codes")` and later calls `recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential(realm, user, credentialModel)` with no null check. If `getProvider(...)` returns null (e.g., provider not registered/feature disabled), the fallback path (when `updateCredential(...)` returns false) will throw a NullPointerException.

adjudication_records.issue_text: server-spi-private/src/main/java/org/keycloak/utils/CredentialHelper.java:118 — IOException from JsonSerialization.writeValueAsString is wrapped in an unchecked RuntimeException and propagates through the required-action flow during login/credential setup, surfacing as a generic 500 instead of a graceful user-facing error

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential(...)` which serializes `generatedCodes` via `JsonSerialization.writeValueAsString(generatedCodes)` and on `IOException` immediately `throw new RuntimeException(e);` (new code around line ~118). This method is invoked from `RecoveryAuthnCodesAction.processAction(...)` during the required-action flow (`createRecoveryCodesCredential(...)` call replaces a direct provider call), and there is no local handling there, so any such exception would propagate and likely become a generic server error. However, with `generatedCodes` being a simple `List<String>`, an `IOException` is unlikely in normal operation, making this primarily a robustness/UX error-handling concern rather than a clearly reproducible functional defect from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/forms/login/freemarker/model/RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean.java:20 — RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) Optional is unwrapped with .get() without presence check, so a user reaching the recovery-code login step without a stored credential (race/inconsistent state) throws NoSuchElementException while rendering the login page

adjudication.rationale: In `RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean` the code now does `Optional<CredentialModel> credentialModelOpt = RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user);` and immediately unwraps it with `credentialModelOpt.get()` when building `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel`. If `getCredential(user)` returns `Optional.empty()` (no recovery-codes credential in federated or local storage), this will throw `NoSuchElementException` during page model creation/rendering. The diff shows no presence check or fallback handling.

adjudication_records.issue_text: server-spi-private/src/main/java/org/keycloak/utils/CredentialHelper.java:113 — createRecoveryCodesCredential has no error handling around user.credentialManager().updateCredential(recoveryCodesCredential); an exception thrown by the user-storage provider's update call is not caught, so the fallback to local credential creation never executes and the required action fails outright instead of falling back gracefully

adjudication.rationale: In the added method `CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential(...)`, the call `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(recoveryCodesCredential)` is not wrapped in any try/catch, so any exception thrown there would abort the method and prevent the intended fallback path (`recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential(...)`) from running. The diff does show this lack of defensive handling; however, the diff does not establish that `updateCredential` can/does throw in normal operation (it returns a boolean and may be expected to propagate provider errors), so this is a robustness/behavioral edge-case concern rather than a verifiable defect from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: server-spi/src/main/java/org/keycloak/models/utils/RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.java:50 — getCredential() silently falls back from federated to stored credentials with no logging/handling if both streams throw (e.g. underlying storage errors), making failures hard to diagnose in production login flows

adjudication.rationale: In the diff, `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(UserModel user)` simply queries `user.credentialManager().getFederatedCredentialsStream()` and, only if no credential is found (`Optional` empty), falls back via `Optional.or(...)` to `getStoredCredentialsByTypeStream(...)`. There is no try/catch or suppression of exceptions; if either underlying stream access throws (e.g., storage error), the exception would propagate rather than being silently handled. The finding’s claim about “silently falls back … if both streams throw” is not supported by the shown code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: testsuite/.../BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.java:335 — Recovery code validation uses `generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(...)` but never removes/marks the matched code as consumed, allowing the same one-time recovery code to be reused indefinitely for login; test-only provider but establishes the pattern userStorage-backed providers must follow

adjudication.rationale: In `BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid(...)`, the new Recovery Codes branch deserializes the stored list and returns `generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse()))` without updating `myUser.recoveryCodes` to remove/mark the matched code as used. From the diff alone, this makes a successful recovery code reusable indefinitely for this user-storage implementation, which violates one-time recovery code semantics and is a real correctness/security defect introduced by the change (even if in a test provider).

adjudication_records.issue_text: testsuite/integration-arquillian/tests/base/src/test/java/org/keycloak/testsuite/federation/storage/BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorageTest.java:241 — testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin only exercises a single successful login and never verifies a used recovery code is rejected/invalidated on reuse

adjudication.rationale: The new test `testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin` only sets up recovery codes, performs a single successful login using one code (`enterRecoveryCodes(...); clickSignInButton(); appPage.assertCurrent();`), and then logs out. There is no subsequent attempt to log in again with the same recovery code to verify one-time-use semantics (rejection/invalidation on reuse). This is a specific, diff-grounded gap in coverage for the newly added recovery-codes flow changes, not a directly verifiable product defect from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: testsuite/integration-arquillian/tests/base/src/test/java/org/keycloak/testsuite/federation/storage/BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorageTest.java:439 — assertUserDontHaveDBCredentials/assertUserHasRecoveryKeysCredentialInUserStorage are mock/state assertions on the test provider's in-memory map rather than assertions of authenticator behavior, so the single test conflates storage-location verification with actual login-flow correctness

adjudication.rationale: In the new test `testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin`, storage-location checks are done via (a) `assertUserDontHaveDBCredentials()` which inspects `user.credentialManager().getStoredCredentialsStream()` (local Keycloak DB) and (b) `assertUserHasRecoveryKeysCredentialInUserStorage()` which calls `BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorageFactory.hasRecoveryCodes("otp1")`, i.e., peeks into the test provider’s internal in-memory map (`userPasswords`). That does verify the test provider’s state, but it’s not an external/behavioral assertion via Keycloak credential APIs for federated creds, so it’s a test-design concern/brittleness rather than a product bug. Also, the test *does* exercise authenticator behavior by completing a login using a recovery code (`enterRecoveryCodes(...)` and `appPage.assertCurrent()`), so the finding’s claim that it’s "rather than assertions of authenticator behavior" is overstated.
